big_idea: Long-term achievement depends less on innate talent than on grit, the combination of sustained passion and perseverance toward long-term goals, and grit can be deliberately cultivated.

tool.label: The grit formula
tool.text: Duckworth models achievement in two steps: Talent times Effort equals Skill, then Skill times Effort equals Achievement, meaning effort counts twice, so it mathematically outweighs raw talent in determining results.
tool.note: This is Duckworth's own simplified model built to make a psychological point vividly, not a peer-reviewed formula; critics note it's illustrative rather than literally tested.

ideas.title: Grit equals passion plus perseverance
ideas.text: Sustained, focused commitment to a single long-term goal matters more than raw giftedness.

ideas.title: The four psychological assets
ideas.text: Gritty people share interest, genuine enjoyment; practice, deliberate daily improvement; purpose, belief the work matters to others; and hope, belief that effort can improve outcomes after setbacks.

ideas.title: Deliberate practice
ideas.text: Grit is expressed through targeted, effortful practice on weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just putting in hours.

ideas.title: Talent is overrated, relatively
ideas.text: People consistently overvalue naturals over hard workers even while claiming to believe the opposite.

ideas.title: Grit can be grown
ideas.text: Through both cultivating interest, practice, purpose, and hope from the inside, and through culture, mentors, and demanding-but-supportive parenting from the outside.

ideas.title: The hard thing rule
ideas.text: Duckworth's own family rule: everyone must do one hard, deliberately practiced thing and can't quit mid-commitment period, but can choose what that thing is.

try_it: Write down your single long-term goal and one hard thing you'll commit to for the next 3 months without quitting.
Schedule 20 minutes of deliberate practice this week on the specific weak point of a skill you're building, with a way to get feedback.
Write one sentence connecting your current work to how it helps someone else.
Track one small daily win related to your goal for 7 days to build the habit of seeing effort produce results.
best_for: People chasing a long-term goal who need motivation to keep going
Parents, coaches, and managers interested in developing perseverance in others
less_useful: Readers wanting a general anti-procrastination or daily productivity toolkit rather than long-horizon commitment
Skeptics of self-help psychology, since the book's core research has drawn published academic criticism about effect size and predictive power

related.why: A closer look at what genuine toughness requires, versus grit's passion-and-perseverance frame
The belief system that underlies whether effort feels worth sustaining
